title: Early Identification and Intervention
summary: Every child is unique and the pace of development varies, but marked difficulties in one or more areas need special care. Disability is any limitation or restriction in performing developmentally appropriate activities expected by society. The ICF-CY describes disability as neither purely biological nor social but the interaction of health conditions, environmental and personal factors, at three levels: impairment in body function or structure (e.g. a cataract), limitation in activity (inability to read or move) and restriction in participation (exclusion from school).

Sensory impairment: loss or impairment of the senses — hearing, vision, speech, smell. Developmental disabilities: chronic conditions from mental or physical impairment, such as Autism Spectrum Disorder, Cerebral Palsy, Down syndrome and Asperger syndrome. Learning disability: impairment of cognitive abilities affecting input (visual or auditory processing), integration, storage (memory) or output (expression); the biggest challenge is that it is hard to identify and diagnose. Behavioural issues: children find it hard to respond to usual care and discipline — ADHD, Oppositional Defiant Disorder, Conduct Disorder — often first taken to be 'difficult' or 'temperamental'. Mental and psychological conditions: intellectual disorders (early symptoms, easier to diagnose) and psychological ones like anxiety, chronic depression and mood swings (detected later). Medical conditions: weakening chronic illnesses such as heart disease, muscular dystrophy and cancer, with long periods of poor health, tests and hospital stays.

Early identification is recognising any disability or developmental variation in the early years and understanding the need for early intervention. It can greatly reduce social, behavioural and learning difficulties. Preschool and kindergarten teachers are at an advantageous position to catch early signs, and should share their observations with parents and specialists. Its purpose is to find which children have developmental problems that may be obstacles to learning or put them at risk. Early development varies widely in rate and pattern, and no clear line can yet be drawn between children whose problems will persist and those who will catch up — so 'wait and see' is not advised; screening and help should be given while the brain is most able to change. Children thought less intelligent may simply have a different learning style. Identification is everyone's responsibility — parents, teachers and caregivers.

Warning signs: oral language (late talking, pronunciation problems, slow vocabulary growth, trouble finding words or following one-step directions, rhyming, no interest in stories); reading and writing (slow naming of objects and colours, weak phonological and print awareness, trouble learning letters and letter-sound links); cognition (trouble memorising the alphabet, numbers or days of the week, poor memory for routines, difficulty with cause and effect, sequencing, counting, size, shape, colour); motor skills (clumsiness, poor balance, trouble with beads, laces and buttons, running, jumping or climbing); social behaviour (trouble playing with others, easy frustration, tantrums, distractibility, impulsiveness, hyperactivity, difficulty with changes in routine).

Strategies: the National Policy for Persons with Disabilities (2006) asks that children up to six be identified early so they can join inclusive education at the right age. The process: (1) screening — finding the areas where a child needs help; (2) checking risk indicators (environmental, biological, genetic, prenatal conditions linked to poor outcomes; they warn but do not always predict) and protective factors (special schools, educators, therapists that reduce risk and build resilience); (3) systematic observation over time in different settings, noting frequency, consistency and severity; (4) comprehensive evaluation by professionals to find the child's pattern of abilities and needs and plan strategies.

Early intervention means doing things as early as possible to work on the child's developmental, health and support needs, generally from birth until five, through specialists such as special educators, therapists and counsellors. Services: screening and assessment, speech and language therapy, physical or occupational therapy, psychological services, home visits, medical, nursing or nutrition services, audiology and vision services, social work and transport. Advantages: better developmental, social and educational gains; less isolation and stress for families; fewer behaviour problems; children grow into productive, independent adults; lower future costs of special education and health care.

Strategies: intensive, good-quality intervention works best; parents and teachers are the first interventionists; no single programme suits every child; regular assessment tracks progress. Occupational therapy helps fine motor, play and self-help skills (dressing, toileting); physiotherapy helps balance, sitting, crawling and walking; speech therapy helps speech, language, eating and drinking. Peer interaction, prompts, modelling and intermittent reinforcement also work. Quality interventions are family-centred (family works with professionals; flexible setting; support), developmentally appropriate (designed for the disability, trained staff, an individual plan for each child reviewed regularly), child-focused (practise skills in different settings, mix with peers) and supportive and structured (a comfortable, supportive environment that is well organised, regular and predictable).

Assistive technology is any item, equipment or product system used to increase, maintain or improve the functional capabilities of persons with disabilities; it improves independence, participation and well-being and can prevent secondary conditions such as deformities. Examples: mobility aids (wheelchairs, walkers, crutches, prosthetic and orthotic devices), hearing aids, Braille, audio recorders and screen readers, cognitive aids, voice recognition and screen enlargement software, page turners, book holders and pencil grips, ramps, grab bars and wide doorways, adaptive utensils and switches, protective headgear, pressure-relief cushions, communication boards. Barriers: lack of awareness, lack of governance (legislation, policies, programmes), lack of services nearby and lack of products. Parents are the primary interventionists, with school staff giving support.

objective: Fill in the blanks: (i) Children with ________ issues may experience difficulty in responding to the regular forms of care and discipline. (ii) Many people with disabilities and their families have ________ awareness of assistive products and services.
Answer in one sentence: As an ECCE teacher, mention one intervention you would take for a child having difficulty in reading and writing.

For example: give extra sound- and visual-discrimination games, rhymes and letter-sound matching in small steps with picture cards, observe the child systematically, share the concern with parents and refer the child to a special educator for assessment.

Answer in one sentence: (i) What is screening? (ii) What are risk indicators?

(i) Determining the areas where children need assistance. (ii) Environmental, biological, genetic and prenatal conditions associated with adverse developmental outcomes — warning signs of a possible disability.

case.passage: Pre-school and kindergarten teachers are at an advantageous position to catch the early signs and symptoms of a developmental delay or disability and to identify children who are at risk in learning and school. Teachers need to be aware of symptoms and share their observations and concerns with parents and other specialists. The purpose of early identification is to determine which children have developmental problems that may be obstacles to learning or that place children at risk. Development in early childhood years is characterised by broad variability in rates and patterns of maturation. At present, no clear distinction can be made in the early years between children whose problems may persist and those who will make adequate progress with time. Therefore, young children who demonstrate difficulties in early development may or may not be at risk for learning disabilities.
items: What is the purpose of early identification mentioned in the passage?
To determine which children have developmental problems that may be obstacles to learning or that place them at risk.
Fill in the blanks: ________ and ________ teachers play a crucial role in identifying developmental delays in young children.
What should teachers do if they observe symptoms of developmental delay?
Share their observations and concerns with parents and other specialists.
Fill in the blanks: In early childhood, development is characterised by broad variability in ________ and ________ of maturation.
What is the challenge in the early identification of developmental problems in young children?
No clear distinction can yet be made between children whose problems will persist and those who will make adequate progress with time.
Is every young child with early difficulties at risk for learning disabilities?
No — such children may or may not be at risk; but screening and support should still be given.

vsa: What are learning disabilities, and what is the biggest challenge for an ECCE teacher in identifying them?

A learning disability is an impairment of cognitive abilities that shows as difficulty in learning — in taking in, integrating, storing or expressing information. The biggest challenge is that learning disabilities are hard to identify and diagnose, since all young children make mistakes and development varies widely.
Why is early identification of disabilities in children important? How can a teacher identify children with difficulty in reading and writing?

Early identification allows help while the young brain is most able to change, and greatly reduces later social, behavioural and learning difficulties. Signs of reading and writing difficulty: slow naming of objects and colours, weak rhyming and syllable blending, little interest in print, trouble learning letters and letter-sound connections.
What intervention therapies can be used for children with disability?

Occupational therapy (fine motor, play and self-help skills like dressing and toileting), physiotherapy (balance, sitting, crawling, walking) and speech therapy (speech, language, eating and drinking), along with psychological services and special education.

Children with disabling health conditions or impairments — from birth or as a result of illness, poor nutrition or injury — who face limitations in activity and restrictions in participation, such as exclusion from school.

vsa: Distinguish mental and psychological conditions from medical conditions.

Mental and psychological conditions affect the mind: intellectual disorders such as delayed mental development, and psychological disorders such as anxiety, chronic depression and mood swings. Medical conditions are weakening chronic physical illnesses such as heart disease, muscular dystrophy and cancer, with long periods of poor health, tests and hospital stays.
sa: What steps would you take to provide early intervention at an ECCE centre? Mention any three.

Any three: observe children systematically and screen them to find who needs help; share concerns with parents and refer the child for comprehensive evaluation by specialists; make an individual plan with the family and specialists and review it regularly; arrange therapy — occupational, physio or speech — and special educators; use child-focused strategies such as peer interaction, prompts, modelling and reinforcement in a supportive, structured, predictable environment; provide assistive devices and barrier-free access.
Explain the developmentally appropriate characteristics of quality interventions.

A developmentally appropriate intervention is specially designed for children in relation to their disability; it has staff specially trained in the intervention and services they give; it develops an individual plan for each child and reviews it regularly; and it tracks the child's progress through regular assessments.
How can assistive technologies support inclusion?

Assistive technology increases, maintains or improves the functioning of children with disabilities, helping them move (wheelchairs, walkers), hear (hearing aids), see and read (Braille, screen readers, enlargement software), communicate (communication boards) and take part in learning (pencil grips, book holders, ramps). It increases independence and participation in school, play and family life, can prevent secondary conditions, and lets children who cannot attend school learn from home through ICT.
What are the barriers to easy access to assistive technologies?

Lack of awareness — many people with disabilities and their families know little about assistive products and services. Lack of governance — weak legislation, policies and national programmes; it is a low priority for many states. Lack of services — few services, often far from where children live. Lack of products — little or no production, with a small range of types, models and sizes.
la: Discuss the strategies for early identification of children with disabilities.

National policies, such as the National Policy for Persons with Disabilities (2006), ask that children up to six be identified at the earliest so they can join inclusive education at the right age. The process: (1) Screening — a system to identify, locate and evaluate children who need early intervention, finding the areas where they need help. (2) Risk indicators and protective factors — environmental, biological, genetic and prenatal conditions that warn of possible problems (but do not always predict them), weighed against protective factors such as special schools, educators and therapists that reduce risk and build resilience. (3) Systematic observation — informal or standard observations repeated over time at home, preschool and play, recording how often, how consistently and how severely the behaviour occurs. (4) Comprehensive evaluation — when risk is suspected, professionals evaluate periodically across settings and perspectives to find the child's pattern of abilities and needs and plan strategies and resources. Teachers should watch for warning signs in language, reading and writing, cognition, motor skills and social behaviour, and share them with parents.
What is early intervention? Describe its advantages and the characteristics of quality interventions.

Early intervention means doing things as early as possible to work on a child's developmental, health and support needs, usually from birth to five, through services such as screening, speech, physical and occupational therapy, psychological, medical and nutrition services, home visits and social work. Advantages: better developmental, social and educational gains; less isolation, stress and frustration for families; fewer behaviour problems through positive strategies; children grow into productive, independent adults; lower future costs of special education and health care. Quality interventions are: family-centred — family works alongside professionals, flexible setting, support and guidance; developmentally appropriate — designed for the disability, trained staff, individual plans reviewed regularly, progress tracked; child-focused — practise skills in different settings, mix with peers; supportive and structured — a comfortable, well-organised, regular and predictable environment.
